# Paper Plaine

> arXiv research papers explained in plain English, updated twice daily.

## What this site is

Paper Plaine surfaces fresh academic research from Cornell University's arXiv preprint database and translates it into plain English for general audiences. Every paper gets three things: a plain-language subtitle (8–12 words capturing the core idea), a 2–3 sentence summary leading with what was found, and a "why it matters" explanation focused on real-world consequences.

The site currently has 986 papers in its archive across 9 subject areas: AI, Computer Science, Physics, Mathematics, Biology, Finance, Statistics, Engineering, Economics. New papers are added automatically twice daily (7 AM and 7 PM UTC). Only first-version arXiv submissions from the past 30 days are considered. Papers are scored for quality signals: venue acceptance (NeurIPS, ICML, Nature, PNAS, etc.), cross-disciplinary listings, and appropriate length.

## How content is structured

Each paper entry contains:
- Formal arXiv title and authors
- Plain-English subtitle — a one-phrase translation of the paper's core idea
- Summary — 2–3 sentences leading with the finding, not the method
- Why it matters — real-world consequences, stated directly
- Link to the full paper on arXiv
- Category and posting date

## Site structure

- Home / archive: https://paperplaine.com (paginated, 12 papers per page)
- Per-category pages: https://paperplaine.com/<category-slug>
- Per-paper pages: https://paperplaine.com/papers/<slug>
- RSS feed: https://paperplaine.com/feed.xml
- llms.txt (this file): https://paperplaine.com/llms.txt
- llms-full.txt (full text of recent papers): https://paperplaine.com/llms-full.txt
- Sitemap: https://paperplaine.com/sitemap.xml

## 10 most recent papers

### FDE-Gym: The Last Mile of AI Delivery
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/fde-gym-the-last
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Dongxu Yang, Hongda Yan, Renxin Wang et al.
- arXiv: 2610.22350
- Plain-English subtitle: Why AI agents struggle when customers don't know what they actually need
- Summary: AI agents that excel at well-defined lab tasks fail dramatically in real customer work, solving only 14 percent of realistic delivery problems. The main culprit is uncovering hidden constraints — what customers didn't mention because they didn't know to mention it — but even when agents gather all the facts, most still can't turn that knowledge into working solutions.
- Why it matters: As companies deploy AI to solve actual business problems, this gap between benchmark performance and real-world delivery directly impacts whether customers get value or disappointment. The benchmark shows that today's best AI agents reach only 56 percent effectiveness on realistic tasks, meaning organizations betting on AI for complex customer work are likely to see failed projects and wasted investment until these systems learn to ask better questions and reason through messy, incomplete information.

### On the fairness of single round-robin tournaments: Evidence from European football
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/on-the-fairness-of
- Category: Economics
- Authors: László Csató, Diána Ivett Fűrész, Zsolt Havran
- arXiv: 2610.21296
- Plain-English subtitle: Why football's uneven home-away schedules don't unfairly tilt league outcomes
- Summary: Single round-robin football tournaments give some teams more home games than others, which theory suggests is unfair. But analysis of European leagues shows this scheduling imbalance has no meaningful effect on final points, despite team strength being the dominant factor—suggesting either the problem is overblown or how experts measure home-field advantage needs rethinking.
- Why it matters: Most sports leagues spend resources and complexity adopting double round-robin formats to eliminate this perceived unfairness. If the problem doesn't actually matter on the field, leagues could simplify their schedules and cut administrative costs without affecting competitive integrity. This also suggests the football analytics community should reconsider how they model home advantage in rating systems.

### From Signals to Evidence: Interpretable Underwater Acoustic Target Sensing with Large Language Models - Part I: Framework and Recognition
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/from-signals-to-evidence
- Category: Engineering
- Authors: Yuge Zhang, Jie Chen, Zhengqiao Zhao et al.
- arXiv: 2610.22064
- Plain-English subtitle: Teaching AI to explain what it hears underwater, not just guess
- Summary: Researchers combined underwater sound analysis with large language models to build a system that doesn't just identify ships—it explains what physical evidence led to that identification. The system can accurately recognize vessels and estimate specific acoustic signatures like shaft frequency and blade-passing frequency, grounded in actual physics rather than black-box pattern matching.
- Why it matters: Navy and coast guard systems currently flag acoustic targets without explaining why, making it hard for operators to trust alerts or learn from mistakes. This framework could turn sonar into a tool that shows its reasoning—identifying a specific ship class while pointing to the exact acoustic features that clinched the call. That transparency matters for training personnel, catching false alarms, and building confidence in automated ocean surveillance.

### MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model for Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/mlexpert-towards-a-generalist
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Shangheng Du, Jinxin Shi, Shuaiyu Zhang et al.
- arXiv: 2610.22344
- Plain-English subtitle: Teaching AI to autonomously design and improve machine learning systems
- Summary: Researchers trained MLExpert, a specialized AI model, to autonomously run machine learning experiments and improve its own optimization strategies based on what it learns. On a standard benchmark, MLExpert nearly doubled the success rate of its base model—from 38% to 73%—matching the performance of much larger frontier AI systems, and its learned skills transferred to other optimization tasks beyond its training domain.
- Why it matters: As AI systems increasingly optimize themselves rather than waiting for human engineers to improve them, this work demonstrates a practical path toward AI that can accelerate its own development cycles. This could compress months of experimentation into days, making advanced AI capabilities faster and cheaper to build—but also raising questions about oversight as these systems operate with less human intervention.

### Language Is a Security Surface for Agent Guards
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/language-is-a-security
- Category: Computer Science
- Authors: Hasan Demirkiran, Jens Ernstberger
- arXiv: 2610.22244
- Plain-English subtitle: Why AI safety guards fail when users speak other languages
- Summary: Security systems that guard AI agents from harmful actions change their safety decisions based on the language a user speaks — even when the actual request and actions remain identical. On rare languages like Amharic, smaller safety guards flip their verdicts up to 4.4 percentage points more often than expected by chance, while the most powerful frontier models like Gemini remain nearly unaffected.
- Why it matters: AI agents are increasingly deployed globally, but their safety mechanisms appear engineered and tested almost entirely in English. A user in a non-English-speaking country could ask the same question that would be blocked in English and have it approved in their own language, potentially exposing them to harmful outputs. This gap widens for smaller, open-source guards that organizations with fewer resources might deploy, creating a security risk that grows with linguistic distance from English.

### Statistical Mechanics of Spike Trains: Self-Consistent Activity Ensembles and Phase Transitions
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/statistical-mechanics-of-spike
- Category: Quantitative Biology
- Authors: Jan Pyrzowski, Laura Messio, Guillaume Marrelec et al.
- arXiv: 2610.20971
- Plain-English subtitle: How brains switch between steady and rhythmic firing modes
- Summary: Researchers developed a physics-based framework for understanding when populations of neurons oscillate versus fire steadily, treating entire sequences of neural spikes as energy states similar to how physicists model physical matter. The model reveals that brain activity undergoes a phase transition—like water freezing into ice—where a competition between synaptic rules and random noise shifts neurons from one firing pattern to a completely different one.
- Why it matters: Understanding these transitions could explain abnormal brain rhythms in epilepsy, sleep disorders, and neuropsychiatric conditions, where the brain gets stuck in pathological oscillations or fails to generate normal rhythmic activity like sleep spindles. The framework provides a new mathematical language for predicting when and why these shifts happen, potentially guiding development of therapies that nudge neural activity out of harmful states.

### LIBERO-PeRM: Benchmarking Personalized Robotic Manipulation
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/libero-perm-benchmarking-personalized
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Zhixu Li, Keqian Tang, Litian Gong et al.
- arXiv: 2610.22372
- Plain-English subtitle: Teaching robots to work the way individual people prefer, not just complete tasks
- Summary: Researchers created the first standardized test for teaching robots to follow human preferences—like choosing a smooth motion over a fast one, or organizing items in a particular way. Current AI-powered robots fail at this when given no examples, but can learn preferences from a handful of demonstrations; however, they struggle to apply what they learned to new layouts or handle conflicting preferences.
- Why it matters: Household robots need to adapt to how different people want tasks done, not just whether tasks get done. Without benchmarks and training data for preference learning, companies building these robots have no way to measure progress or know which approaches actually work. This benchmark gives the field a shared standard to build better robots that respect individual styles and habits.

### Convergence Rates for Lasserre's Upper-Bound Hierarchy on \mathbb{R}^d with Gaussian Measure
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/convergence-rates-for-lasserre
- Category: Mathematics
- Authors: Sander Gribling, Igor Klep, Poornendu Kumar
- arXiv: 2610.22030
- Plain-English subtitle: Finding the bottom of a mountain using progressively better mathematical approximations
- Summary: Mathematicians proved how fast a computational tool called Lasserre's hierarchy can narrow in on the lowest point of any polynomial function—showing it gets closer by roughly a factor of 1/r with each step of refinement. This is the first explicit speed guarantee for this method when the search space is infinite, and the researchers proved this rate cannot be improved in general.
- Why it matters: Optimization problems—finding the best solution to a constraint—appear constantly in engineering, finance, and machine learning. This result gives practitioners a concrete guarantee: if you apply this method 100 times, you'll be roughly 100 times closer to the true answer than after just one iteration. Knowing this rate helps decide when to stop computing and accept the current best answer.

### Query-Efficient Rejection Sampling for Parallel Masked Diffusion
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/query-efficient-rejection-sampling
- Category: Statistics
- Authors: Shiyuan Zhang, Xuheng Li, Qiwei Di et al.
- arXiv: 2610.22238
- Plain-English subtitle: Speeding up AI text generation without sacrificing quality or needing excessive computations
- Summary: When AI models generate multiple words at once to speed things up, they typically ignore how those words relate to each other, producing biased results. Researchers developed SIRS, a new method that corrects this bias while requiring dramatically fewer computational checks—just one query instead of one per token—by cleverly reusing information the model already computes.
- Why it matters: Faster, more accurate text generation directly reduces computational costs and energy use in AI systems while improving output quality. This matters for large-scale applications like real-time translation, chatbots, and content generation, where speed and accuracy improvements compound across millions of queries.

### Recovering Reliable Supervision via Critique-Guided On-Policy Distillation
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/recovering-reliable-supervision-via
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Kaixiang Zhao, Tianrun Yu, Shangzhe Li et al.
- arXiv: 2610.20572
- Plain-English subtitle: Training AI to fix its mistakes by learning from its own corrections
- Summary: When teaching an AI model to solve problems by learning from its own attempts, a major flaw emerges: the teacher model gets pulled along into the student's mistakes instead of correcting course. Researchers developed CriticOPD, which has the teacher identify where the student went wrong, then watches the student rewrite the solution correctly—and learning from that revision produces measurably better results, especially on hard competition math problems.
- Why it matters: Most AI systems today struggle with complex reasoning because the feedback they receive during training can't reliably steer them back on track once they start down the wrong path. This method directly addresses that bottleneck by forcing a real correction cycle into the training loop. Better error recovery during training means these models could solve harder problems in the real world without requiring as much human oversight or external correction data.
